title: ColBERT: late interaction and MaxSim
summary: Instead of squashing a passage into one vector, ColBERT keeps one vector per token and scores by finding, for each query word, its best match anywhere in the document. The quality comes free and the storage does not: with 128 dimensional token vectors, the index costs the token count divided by three, which is 372 times bigger on this course's own lessons.
html:
Everything dense we have built so far squashes a whole passage into a single vector. Two hundred words become 384 numbers. That is roughly a hundred to one compression, and the loss is real: if a chunk covers three topics, its one vector points somewhere between all three and matches none of them well. Day 6 circled this from the chunking side, and day 42 comes back to it. ColBERT attacks it from the representation side.

Its answer is to stop squashing. Keep one vector per token, and compare them all.

MaxSim, which is simpler than it sounds

Here is the whole scoring rule. For each word in the query, look at every word in the document, find the one it matches best, and keep that single best score. Then add up those best scores across the query's words.

In plain terms: for each thing I asked about, how well does this document cover it at its strongest point? Then sum over the things I asked about.

Worked on something small. Query: mortgage rate. Document: "the housing loan interest fell sharply".

query word "mortgage"  best match in document: "loan"      0.72
query word "rate"      best match in document: "interest"  0.68
                                                   score =  1.40

Note what did not happen. The document's words "the", "fell" and "sharply" contributed nothing and diluted nothing. In a single vector world, all six words get averaged into one representation, and the three irrelevant ones drag it away from the query. Here a match only has to exist somewhere, and nothing is averaged away.

That is why ColBERT is strong exactly where single vectors are weak: long passages, and chunks that cover more than one subject.

Why it is called late interaction

Three ways to let a query and a document meet, and the only difference is when.

No interaction until the very end. Encode the query to one vector, encode the document to one vector, compare the two numbers at the end. This is everything from days 9 to 14. Cheap, and you can encode every document once, in advance, at ingest time.

Interaction from the start. Feed the query and the document into the model together, as one input, and let every word see every other word the whole way through. Most accurate by a clear margin. Completely unprecomputable, because the model's work depends on the pair, so you cannot touch your corpus until the query arrives. That is tomorrow's lesson.

Interaction after encoding, at the token level. ColBERT. Encode separately, so you can still precompute the whole corpus, but keep the tokens so the comparison can be fine grained. "Late" means after encoding rather than during it.

It really is trying to have both, and it mostly succeeds. The bill arrives in storage.

The storage bill, exactly

A single vector for a 200 token chunk, 384 dimensions at 4 bytes each, is 1,536 bytes. ColBERT keeps a 128 dimensional vector per token, so the same chunk costs 200 times 128 times 4, which is 102,400 bytes. Sixty seven times more.

And there is a tidy way to see it. The ratio is tokens times 128 over 384, which is just the token count divided by three. Your ColBERT index is bigger than your single vector index by the number of tokens in a chunk, divided by three. Nothing else matters.

chunk size    single vector    ColBERT fp32      ratio
  200 tokens        1,536 B        102,400 B        67x
  512 tokens        1,536 B        262,144 B       171x
1,128 tokens        1,536 B        577,536 B       376x

In practice nobody stores fp32. Quantise each dimension down to 2 bits, which is what the PLAID work does, and you divide by 16, bringing a 200 token chunk to about 6,400 bytes, four times the single vector rather than sixty seven. Still more, and now tolerable.

The analogy: a single vector is the one line summary of a document. ColBERT keeps an index card per word. Answering a question, you check your question against the best card for each part of it. Better answers, a much bigger filing cabinet.

If you want to see it measured

This is exact arithmetic on the real corpus rather than an estimate. The 35 lessons of this course are 39,084 tokens in total, averaging 1,117 tokens each.

single vector index, 384 dims      52 KB
ColBERT index, 128 dims per token  19.1 MB     372x
same, quantised to 2 bits per dim   1.19 MB     23x

372 is exactly 1,117 divided by three, which is the rule from above landing on real data. The reason the multiplier is so ugly here is that these lessons are long documents. Chunk them to 200 tokens first, as any real system would, and you are back to 67x before quantisation.

What I have not shown you

I have not run ColBERT. The published results have it beating single vector dense retrieval on quality fairly consistently, and landing close to cross-encoder reranking at much lower query cost. Treat that as reported.

Two honest caveats. You cannot drop ColBERT into an ordinary vector database, because there is no simple top-k over per-token vectors: you need a separate candidate generation stage, which is most of what PLAID is about and most of why adoption lags the quality numbers. And whether ColBERT beats the plainer recipe of BM25 plus dense plus a reranker is unsettled, and mostly comes down to whether your latency budget has room for the reranker.

If you remember one thing
ColBERT keeps one vector per token and scores by best match per query word, so nothing gets averaged away. The index costs your token count divided by three, and quantisation is what makes that survivable.

That closes phase 2. Phase 3 starts tomorrow with bi-encoders versus cross-encoders, which is the precomputation question from the middle of today's lesson, taken seriously.
exercise:
One. Write your day 36 note. Phase 2 ended today, so this is a good one to rate.

Two. Work out the ColBERT index size for your own situation. Pick a corpus you know, say a million chunks of 300 tokens. Single vector at 384 dimensions and 4 bytes is one number, ColBERT at 128 dimensions per token is another, and the 2 bit quantised version is a third. Then ask the real question: which of those three fits in the RAM of a machine you could actually requisition?
